title: High Throughput Phenotyping of Physician Notes with Large Language and Hybrid NLP Models
authors: Syed I. Munzir, Daniel B. Hier, Michael D. Carrithers
text:
Precision medicine entails the precise matching of diagnosis, outcome, treatment, and molecular mechanism of disease to individual patients [1,2]. An important component of precision medicine is the precise description of the signs and symptoms of disease with standardized and computable terms from a suitable ontology [3]. This detailed description of signs and symptoms has been called deep phenotyping. The deep phenotyping of thousands or even millions of physician notes within electronic health records requires high throughput methods [4,3,5]. Although high throughput phenotyping has gained traction in agriculture [6,7], its adoption in human medicine has been slower [5]. Improved methods for high throughput phenotyping of electronic health records are needed for precision medicine [8,9,10].

The extraction of signs and symptoms from electronic health records is a two-step process that involves identification and mapping. Identification finds spans of text that describe the signs and symptoms of the disease, which are then mapped to concepts in a suitable disease ontology and assigned a machine-readable code [11]. Concept extraction (sometimes called concept recognition or concept identification) is closely related to the natural language task of named entity recognition (NER) [12,13,14]. Medical concepts in free text can be extracted manually, but this work is slow, laborious, and tedious.

Natural language processing (NLP) has been searching for methods to automate the extraction of medical concepts from free text. Automation of medical concept extraction makes high throughput phenotyping of electronic health records feasible. Progress towards this goal has been significant, and powerful fifth-generation systems are emerging.

- 1. First-Generation: Dictionary-based and rule-based systems [11,15,16].

- 2. Second-Generation: Machine learning algorithms like conditional random fields, support vector machines, and hidden Markov models [17,18]. Other second-generation systems made important advances in linguistic analysis [19,20].

- 3. Third-Generation: Deep learning models, particularly those using RNNs (Recurrent Neural Networks) and CNNs (Convolutional Neural Networks) [21,22,23,24,25]

- 4. Fourth-Generation: BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) and transformer-based models, introducing the self-attention mechanism. A shift from static word embeddings to context-aware word embeddings that facilitate a deeper understanding of language [26,27,28,29,30,31].

- 5. Fifth-Generation: General-purpose large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4 (Generative Pre-trained Transformer 4), which build upon the transformer architecture to provide more versatility, scalability, and generalizability across a wide range of tasks.

General-purpose large language models, such as GPT-4, are emerging that can perform difficult NLP tasks such as the phenotyping of physician notes [32,33,34] without additional model training.

Experimental Setup. We manually annotated the signs and symptoms (phenotype) in the physician notes of thirty multiple sclerosis patients. Notes were phenotyped by a hybrid model (NimbleMiner) and a general-purpose large language model (GPT-4). The phenotypes created by the two models were compared to the ground truth labels. Performance metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, and precision, were calculated for each model.
